newsitem.title: FRANCE: France confident EU will approve one-off payment.
newsitem.headline: France confident EU will approve one-off payment.

text.p: French government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said on Wednesday he was confident that the European Commission would approve France's controversial decision to use a one-off payment from France Telecom to reduce its budget deficit and help it qualify for European monetary union.
"We have no reason to think the Eurostat decision will be different than what we believe right now," Lamassoure, who is also budget minister, told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
Eurostat is the statistical arm of the European Union executive.

On Tuesday, the franc fell against the mark after reports that an accounting working party had not approved the 37.5 billion franc France Telecom transfer, seen as vital to France reducing its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for monetary union.
French finance ministry officials denied the report.
A European Commission source said on Wednesday that German, British and Dutch officials on the statistics advisory committee had argued against allowing France to use the transfer.
"There was a small minority, two or three countries, that expressed doubts," a spokesman for Economic and Monetary Affairs Commmissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy also said.
But the decision on whether the plan should be allowed would be taken by the director general of Eurostat in the next few days and would be based solely on technical grounds, he said.

The payment by France Telecom is in exchange for the French government assuming the state-owned telephone operator's pension liablities ahead of its partial privatisation but some critics have said the move smacks of "creative accounting".
Earlier, Lamassoure quoted Chirac as pledging at a cabinet meeting that France would meet all deadlines in the drive to create a single European currency.
Chirac also said France and Germany would do everything that must be done to respect the calendar for European Economic and Monetary Union, Lamassoure added.

On Tuesday, six leading German research institutes said Germany would fail to meet in 1997 the Maastricht-treaty criteria for the single currency because its public sector deficit was likely to be 3.5 percent of gross domestic product.
